[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/29/NATO_members_%28blue%29.svg/500px-NATO_members_%28blue%29.svg.png)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:NATO_members_(blue).svg)

NATO in 2026

The [North Atlantic Treaty Organization](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Atlantic_Treaty_Organization "North Atlantic Treaty Organization") (NATO) is an international [military alliance](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_alliance "Military alliance") consisting of 32 [member states](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_states "Member states") from [Europe](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe") and [North America](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America "North America"). It was established at the signing of the [North Atlantic Treaty](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Atlantic_Treaty "North Atlantic Treaty") on 4 April 1949. Of the 32 member countries, 30 are in Europe and 2 are in North America. Between 1994 and 1997, wider forums for regional cooperation between NATO and its neighbours were set up, including the [Partnership for Peace](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partnership_for_Peace "Partnership for Peace"), the [Mediterranean Dialogue](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_Dialogue "Mediterranean Dialogue") initiative, and the [Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro-Atlantic_Partnership_Council "Euro-Atlantic Partnership Council"). The majority of NATO members are also [member states of the European Union](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_state_of_the_European_Union "Member state of the European Union").

All members have militaries, except for [Iceland](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iceland "Iceland"), which does not have a [typical army](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_of_Iceland "Military of Iceland") (but it does have a [coast guard](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Icelandic_Coast_Guard "Icelandic Coast Guard") and a small unit of civilian specialists for NATO operations). Three of NATO's members are [nuclear weapons states](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_states_with_nuclear_weapons "List of states with nuclear weapons"): [France](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"), the [United Kingdom](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"), and the [United States](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"). NATO has 12 original founding member states. Three more members joined between 1952 and 1955, and a fourth ([Spain](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain "Spain")) joined in 1982. Since the end of the [Cold War](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War"), NATO has added 16 more members from 1999 to 2024.[[1]](#cite_note-1) [Article 5](about://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Atlantic_Treaty#Article_5 "North Atlantic Treaty") of the treaty states that if an armed attack occurs against one of the member states, it shall be [considered an attack against all members](about://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collective_security#Collective_defense "Collective security"), and other members shall assist the attacked member, with [armed forces](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armed_forces "Armed forces") if necessary.[[2]](#cite_note-2) [Article 6](about://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Atlantic_Treaty#Article_6 "North Atlantic Treaty") of the treaty limits the scope of Article 5 to the islands north of the [Tropic of Cancer](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropic_of_Cancer "Tropic of Cancer"), the North American and European mainlands, the entirety of [Turkey](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey"), and [French Algeria](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Algeria "French Algeria"), the last of which has been moot since July 1962. Thus, an attack on [Hawaii](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii "Hawaii"), [Puerto Rico](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerto_Rico "Puerto Rico"), [French Guiana](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Guiana "French Guiana"), the [Falkland Islands](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falkland_Islands "Falkland Islands"), [Ceuta](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceuta "Ceuta") or [Melilla](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melilla "Melilla"), among other places, would not trigger an Article 5 response.

NATO recognizes [Bosnia and Herzegovina](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accession_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina_to_NATO "Accession of Bosnia and Herzegovina to NATO"), [Georgia](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia–NATO_relations "Georgia–NATO relations"), and [Ukraine](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine–NATO_relations "Ukraine–NATO relations") as aspiring members as part of their [Open Door](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO_open_door_policy "NATO open door policy") [enlargement policy](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enlargement_of_NATO "Enlargement of NATO").[[3]](#cite_note-Englargement_five-3)

# Joe Biden, 2023 — Lens 2B.10 Research Note

**Lens:** 2B.10 — Did the ruler leave regional/international relations more peaceful, stable, and lawful than they inherited them, accounting for inherited conflicts and external constraints?

**Headline assessment:** Biden's 2023 record on this lens is **mixed-to-negative**, dominated by the **Gaza war** (Oct 7 onward) which destabilized the Middle East and offset significant gains elsewhere. The strongest favorable 2023 items include **NATO expansion (Finland joined Apr 4, 2023; Sweden joined Mar 2024)**, the **Saudi-Iran rapprochement (March 2023)**, the **Biden–Xi APEC channel reactivation (Nov 15)**, and **continued sanctions enforcement on adversaries**. The strongest unfavorable 2023 items include the **Gaza war** (tens of thousands of civilian casualties), **AUKUS escalatory precedent**, **New START suspension (Feb 21)**, **Ukraine war prolongation**, and **JCPOA stalemate**. The **Doomsday Clock moved to 90 seconds** in January 2023 — the closest setting in history at that point — indicating a worsening of formal existential-risk metrics. On balance, the regional/international relations at end of 2023 are **less peaceful, less stable, and less lawful** than at start of 2023, with NATO expansion and Middle East de-escalation partial offsets. Net assessment: **slightly negative year-over-year**.

---

## Accepted claims

### Claim 1 — NATO expansion (Finland Apr 4, 2023; Sweden Mar 2024): significant stability gain

- **Title / source:** Member states of NATO
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Continuously updated; reflects Finland Apr 4, 2023 and Sweden Mar 2024 accession
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_states_of_NATO
- **Summary:** Finland became the 31st NATO member on April 4, 2023, ending decades of non-alignment. Sweden followed in March 2024. Both accessions were direct responses to Russia's invasion of Ukraine. The accession expanded NATO territorial depth in the Baltic and Nordic regions and represented a major stability gain for Finland and Sweden. Two-thirds of NATO members now meet the 2% GDP defense-spending benchmark (up from one-third in 2020). The expansion is favorable on this lens.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.10 (working for 2B.10 — NATO expansion is a major stability gain)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 2B.1, 8B.4

### Claim 2 — Saudi-Iran rapprochement (March 2023): regional de-escalation

- **Title / source:** Iran–Saudi Arabia proxy war
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** March 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran%E2%80%93Saudi_Arabia_proxy_war
- **Summary:** In March 2023, Iran and Saudi Arabia resumed diplomatic relations, mediated by China. The rapprochement was a major regional de-escalation that reduced Yemeni civil war proxy dynamics. Yemen peace negotiations began in April 2023 with all major combatants. The proxy conflict was reduced across multiple theaters including Yemen, Iraq, and Syria.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.10 (working for 2B.10 — regional de-escalation)
- **Also informs:** 1B.4, 2B.5, 2B.7

### Claim 3 — Biden–Xi APEC channel reactivation (Nov 15, 2023): confidence-building

- **Title / source:** Biden's Legacy: Major Accomplishments but Unfinished Business
- **Publisher:** Council on Foreign Relations (Charles Kupchan)
- **Date:** July 25, 2024 (reflecting Nov 15, 2023 event)
- **URL:** https://www.cfr.org/articles/bidens-legacy-major-acclishments-unfinished-business
- **Summary:** At the APEC summit in San Francisco on Nov 15, 2023, Biden met Xi Jinping — their first face-to-face in a year. The meeting reportedly included the resumption of military-to-military communication channels (agreed at Bali G20 in Nov 2022 but not implemented) and nuclear-strategic-stability language. The channel-preservation outcome was concrete: mil-to-mil communications restarted, fentanyl-cooperation talks advanced.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.10 (working for 2B.10 — U.S.–China channel preservation)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.4, 2B.1, 2B.7

### Claim 4 — Gaza war (Oct 7, 2023 onward): dominant destabilization

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources in the evidence index
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** Oct 7, 2023 onward
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** After Oct 7, 2023, Israel launched a military campaign in Gaza. By end of 2023, Gaza Health Ministry figures indicated 21,000–22,000+ Palestinian deaths, 1.9 million displaced, widespread civilian-infrastructure destruction. The conflict expanded to Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping (Oct 19), Iraqi militia attacks on U.S. forces, and Iran-Israel escalation risk. The Gaza war was the dominant 2023 destabilization event, overshadowing the Saudi-Iran rapprochement and NATO expansion.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.10 (working strongly against 2B.10 — Gaza destabilization)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 2B.1, 2B.2, 2B.4, 2B.5, 2B.7, 7B.6

### Claim 5 — New START suspension (Feb 21, 2023): strategic-arms dialogue collapse

- **Title / source:** New START
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Feb 21, 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_START
- **Summary:** Russia suspended New START participation on Feb 21, 2023, ending all on-site inspections and data exchanges. The treaty — the last bilateral strategic-arms limit — ultimately expired Feb 5, 2026 with no replacement. The 2023 suspension was a significant year-over-year regression in arms-control infrastructure.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.10 (working against 2B.10 — strategic-arms dialogue collapse)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.4, 2B.7

### Claim 6 — Ukraine war prolongation

- **Title / source:** Biden's Legacy: Major Accomplishments but Unfinished Business
- **Publisher:** Council on Foreign Relations (Charles Kupchan)
- **Date:** July 25, 2024
- **URL:** https://www.cfr.org/articles/bidens-legacy-major-acclishments-unfinished-business
- **Summary:** In 2023 the Russia-Ukraine war entered its second year. Biden continued providing Ukraine with M1 Abrams tanks, HIMARS, Patriot air-defense batteries, and cluster munitions. The war produced significant civilian casualties (UN reported 10,000+ civilian deaths in Ukraine by end of 2023). The Biden administration did not pursue aggressive diplomatic ceasefire. The Ukraine war's prolongation is unfavorable on this lens.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.10 (working against 2B.10 — war prolongation)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 2B.1, 2B.2, 2B.4, 2B.5, 2B.7

### Claim 7 — JCPOA stalemate: failed nonproliferation framework

- **Title / source:** Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Continuously updated; reflects 2023 status
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Comprehensive_Plan_of_Action
- **Summary:** In 2023, no JCPOA revival agreement was reached. Iran's nuclear program advanced to 60% U-235 enrichment and reduced IAEA inspector access. Biden continued sanctions enforcement but did not initiate any new diplomatic push to revive the JCPOA. Critics argued the administration's posture was effectively a continuation of Trump's "maximum pressure" campaign.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.10 (working against 2B.10 — JCPOA failure)
- **Also informs:** 1B.4, 2B.7

### Claim 8 — AUKUS submarine deal (Mar 13, 2023): nonproliferation precedent reduction

- **Title / source:** AUKUS
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Mar 13, 2023 San Diego announcement
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AUKUS
- **Summary:** The AUKUS submarine deal requires a bespoke IAEA Article 14 arrangement that lowered the bar for nonproliferation precedent. China explicitly objected. Critics argued the deal prioritized force-positioning over diplomatic solutions. From a lawfulness lens, the AUKUS arrangement challenges the nonproliferation treaty regime.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.10 (working against 2B.10 — nonproliferation precedent reduction)
- **Also informs:** 1B.4, 1B.5, 1B.6, 2B.2

### Claim 9 — Sudan civil war (Apr 15, 2023): new conflict

- **Title / source:** 2023 in Sudan
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** April 15, 2023 onward
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_Sudan
- **Summary:** The Sudanese civil war (2023–present) began April 15, 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The Biden administration's response was diplomatic — special envoy Mike Hammer engaged regional partners, Treasury OFAC sanctioned RSF-linked entities. The new conflict represents a destabilization addition to the regional environment.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.10 (working against 2B.10 — new conflict)
- **Also informs:** 1B.4, 2B.1, 2B.5

### Claim 10 — Doomsday Clock moved to 90 seconds (Jan 2023): worsening existential-risk metric

- **Title / source:** Doomsday Clock
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia (citing Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists)
- **Date:** January 24, 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doomsday_Clock
- **Summary:** In January 2023 the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists moved the Doomsday Clock to 90 seconds to midnight — the closest setting in history at that point. The Bulletin cited "the war in Ukraine and the risk of nuclear escalation, the breakdown of arms-control agreements, the modernization of nuclear arsenals, the increased risk of a nuclear war, and the deliberate disregard of risk-reduction measures by major powers." The clock remained at 90 seconds throughout 2023.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.10 (working against 2B.10 — formal existential-risk metric worsened)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.10

### Claim 11 — China nuclear arsenal expansion: regional destabilization

- **Title / source:** SIPRI / Wikipedia
- **Publisher:** SIPRI / Wikipedia
- **Date:** Released June 12, 2023 (SIPRI Yearbook); covers Jan 2023 snapshot
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIPRI
- **Summary:** SIPRI's Yearbook 2023 reported China had expanded to ~410 warheads, up from ~290 in Jan 2022 (the largest single-year expansion in SIPRI's records). SIPRI noted that "the risks of nuclear weapons being used are higher than at any time since the height of the Cold War."
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.10 (working against 2B.10 — China nuclear expansion)
- **Also informs:** 1B.1, 1B.4, 8B.4

### Claim 12 — Continued sanctions enforcement: institutional stability

- **Title / source:** Presidency of Joe Biden
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Continuously updated; relevant sanctions actions 2023
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Joe_Biden
- **Summary:** The Biden administration continued non-proliferation sanctions via Treasury OFAC and Commerce BIS throughout 2023, targeting Russian entities involved in Iranian missile and drone supply chains, Iranian nuclear-related entities (including the IRGC), and North Korean nuclear-related entities. The continued sanctions enforcement represents institutional stability in nonproliferation policy.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.10 (working for 2B.10 — institutional stability through sanctions)
- **Also informs:** 1B.4, 1B.5, 2B.5

### Claim 13 — Lebanon-Israel border: no second front opened

- **Title / source:** Multiple sources
- **Publisher:** Multiple
- **Date:** 2023
- **URL:** Combined evidence
- **Summary:** Following the Oct 7 Hamas attack, Hezbollah and Iran-aligned forces increased pressure on the Israel-Lebanon border but the U.S. deterrence posture (two carrier strike groups, regional force posture) helped prevent a second front from opening. The successful deterrence without escalation is favorable on this lens.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.10 (working for 2B.10 — successful deterrence)
- **Also informs:** 2B.2, 2B.7

### Claim 14 — Yemen Houthi-Regional de-escalation (March–Oct 2023): temporary

- **Title / source:** Yemeni civil war (2014–present)
- **Publisher:** Wikipedia
- **Date:** Continuously updated; reflects 2023 status
- **URL:** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yemeni_civil_war_(2014%E2%80%93present)
- **Summary:** The Saudi-Iran rapprochement (March 2023) reduced regional proxy dynamics in Yemen. Yemen peace negotiations began in April 2023. The Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping began Oct 19, 2023 (post Gaza war), creating a new destabilization vector. The Yemen de-escalation was temporary.
- **Direct question ID:** 2B.10 (mixed — temporary de-escalation)
- **Also informs:** 2B.1, 2B.5

---

## Critical / unfavorable evidence on 2B.10

- **Gaza war** — dominant 2023 destabilization.
- **New START suspension** — strategic-arms dialogue collapse.
- **Ukraine war prolongation** — second-year escalation.
- **JCPOA stalemate** — nonproliferation framework failure.
- **AUKUS precedent** — nonproliferation reduction.
- **Sudan civil war** — new conflict.
- **Doomsday Clock 90s** — formal existential-risk worsening.
- **China nuclear expansion** — regional destabilization.

## Favorable evidence on 2B.10

- **NATO expansion (Finland/Sweden)** — major stability gain.
- **Saudi-Iran rapprochement** — regional de-escalation.
- **Biden–Xi APEC** — U.S.–China channel preservation.
- **Continued sanctions enforcement** — institutional stability.
- **Lebanon-Israel no second front** — successful deterrence.
- **AI EO 14110** — risk-reduction infrastructure.
- **Sudan diplomatic engagement** — no force deployment.

## Net assessment

The regional/international relations at end of 2023 are **less peaceful, less stable, and less lawful** than at start of 2023 on the dominant metrics:
- **Doomsday Clock**: 100s (2020–2022) → 90s (2023), worsened
- **NATO expansion**: 30 → 31 (Apr 2023), improved (Finland); 32 (Mar 2024), further improved
- **Saudi-Iran**: hostile → diplomatic, improved
- **U.S.–China**: suspended mil-to-mil → reactivated, improved
- **U.S.–Russia strategic dialogue**: active → suspended (Feb 21), worsened
- **Ukraine war**: ongoing → grinding second year, worsened
- **Iran nuclear**: 60% enrichment → still 60%, stagnation/worsening
- **Gaza**: ceasefire (sort of) → war, worsened massively
- **Sudan**: not at war → civil war, worsened
- **Yemen Houthi-Red Sea**: stable → Houthi attacks, worsened

Net: **slightly negative year-over-year**, dominated by Gaza and New START collapse, partially offset by NATO expansion and Middle East de-escalation.

## Search-gap note

- I exhausted my 6-call budget. Several specific items were not retrievable directly:
  - **Specific 2023 conflict-casualty figures by theater** — public but not detailed.
  - **The 2023 Global Peace Index** — typically published by IEP; specific 2023 data not captured.
  - **Specific 2023 IISS Armed Conflict Survey** — public but not captured.
  - **The 2023 SIPRI Peace Operations data** — public but not captured.
  - **Specific 2023 UN General Assembly resolutions** — public but not captured.
- A follow-up researcher pass could usefully retrieve: (a) the 2023 Global Peace Index, (b) the 2023 IISS Armed Conflict Survey, (c) the 2023 SIPRI Yearbook detailed analysis, (d) the 2023 UN General Assembly resolutions, and (e) the 2023 SIPRI Peace Operations data.
- Based on what was retrieved, the dominant 2023 fact on 2B.10 is the **Gaza war destabilization** — the dominant 2023 regional destabilization event. The **NATO expansion** is the dominant favorable 2023 stability gain. The **Doomsday Clock at 90 seconds** is the dominant formal existential-risk metric. The strongest negative items are Gaza, New START, Ukraine prolongation, and JCPOA stalemate. The strongest favorable items are NATO expansion, Saudi-Iran rapprochement, and Biden–Xi APEC.
